title: For time-intensive platforms, attention and opportunity cost are part of the consumer price
source_unit: Two Facebook/Instagram field experiments and an economic model reported in NBER Working Paper 34743; platform-user experiment, not a representative welfare panel
geography: United States platform users and online/offline activity alternatives as described by the study

observations.period: 2026; two field experiments on Facebook and Instagram

user_cost_manipulated.value: ad load, described as the primary user cost in the setting

substitution_scope.value: online activities and offline time use

observations.method: NBER working-paper abstract describing two field experiments; this record preserves the experiment count and qualitative result without reconstructing unreported cell-level estimates.
observations.uncertainty: Low response to ad load does not identify whether users value the service highly, lack close substitutes, tolerate ads, or bear a low welfare cost. The abstract does not provide long-run well-being, sleep, work, care, or household outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Users in the Facebook and Instagram field experiments; the public abstract does not provide a representative-population denominator or subgroup estimates.
observations.counterinterpretation: Time spent can be valuable leisure, social connection, or information rather than time lost. Low ad-load elasticity can coexist with high platform benefit or with constrained substitution.

observations.period: 2026; model and competition application in NBER Working Paper 34743

denominator.unit: time-allocation demand model and Federal Trade Commission-proposed de-merger application

competition_counterfactual.value: potential separation of Facebook and Instagram is explored

observations.method: NBER abstract describing the Beckerian time-allocation model and its application to platform competition.
observations.uncertainty: A modeled diversion ratio or de-merger scenario is not an observed separation, price change, welfare realization, or political outcome. The authors disclose that they worked on behalf of Meta in connection with antitrust litigation; Meta did not provide financial support, and the paper states opinions/errors are the authors' own.
observations.subgroup: Model-defined platform activities and users represented in the field experiments; not a national household welfare estimate.
observations.counterinterpretation: Accounting for time can improve competition analysis without implying that a regulator should separate platforms or that users would choose an offline substitute under an actual structural change.

related_sources.claim: NBER identifies the authors, January 2026 issue date, May 2026 revision, field-experiment design, low ad-load elasticity, time-cost substitution, and de-merger application.
Earlier NBER time-intensive-goods work supplies conceptual context for valuing time as part of product cost.
related_sources.access_boundary: The older Internet valuation study is not pooled with the 2026 Facebook/Instagram experiments.

boundary: This record promotes a time-price mechanism for digital consumer demand. It observes experimental response and model application, but does not establish user well-being, household care/work displacement, dependence, practical exit, realized consumer surplus, or the effect of an actual platform separation. The next test is a consented time-use and substitution panel with platform exposure, ad load, content value, offline activity, work/care/sleep, switching, and later trust kept separate.
